annualCost.label: Yearly federal costs, from the published accounts
annualCost.note: Re-sample after each fiscal year closes. Each item carries its own source. The federal-spending card must equal totalOutlays in outlays.json; validation enforces it.

price.label: Unit costs the government publishes for its own purchases
price.note: Each item carries its own source. A weapon price moves with the contract, not the calendar, so record the budget year in the note.

total.label: Lump sums, counted once and still running
total.note: These are cumulative totals, not yearly rates. They only grow. The site divides them across every US household.

households.label: Number of US households, Census Bureau
households.note: The denominator for every household-share card. Families and Living Arrangements tables, table HH-1.

groups.title: The scale of it
groups.lede: Your whole working life, laid against one year of federal spending. The unit is the second.

groups.title: Pissed away
groups.lede: This is money that bought nothing at all.

groups.title: Stolen outright
groups.lede: Not wasted. Taken. Every figure here comes from the government's own investigators.

groups.title: Nobody can say where it went
groups.lede: The money left. The receipts cannot be produced, and in most cases nobody was held to account.

groups.title: Prices only a government pays
groups.lede: One thing, bought once, at a price no buyer spending their own money would agree to.

groups.title: Bought in your name
groups.lede: Not frivolous. Deliberate. Your share of what the money was used to do.

groups.title: The defence they always make
groups.lede: The programmes people name first when they defend the tax. Here is what the people who run them publish about them.

items.label: of all federal spending
items.note: Outlays were $7.01 trillion in the 2025 fiscal year, from Treasury's own closed accounts. That is what your life's work bought at the till.

source.label: Final Monthly Treasury Statement, FY2025, total outlays

items.label: of interest on the national debt
items.note: Three numbers describe this and they are not the same. Treasury as a department spent $1,458.9 billion, which is the slice you see in the donut above. Gross interest on the debt alone was $1,215.6 billion. Net of what the government pays its own trust funds, CBO puts the cost near $970 billion. This card uses the smallest of the three. Even at the smallest, it buys nothing. It is rent on money already spent.

source.label: CBO, Monthly Budget Review, fiscal year 2025

items.label: of the deficit on its own
items.note: The 2025 shortfall was $1.8 trillion. That part was borrowed, not taxed, so no tax receipt covers it. It is deferred tax. The bill goes to whoever is working when it comes due, with interest on top, and many of them cannot vote yet. Read every share on this page as a share of what was spent, not of what was collected.

source.label: CBO, Monthly Budget Review, fiscal year 2025

items.label: of payments the government admits were wrong
items.note: Fifteen agencies reported $186 billion of improper payments in 2025, across 64 programmes. The running total since 2003 is about $3 trillion.

source.label: GAO-26-108694, Payment Integrity

items.label: federal agencies used a quarter or less of their headquarters
items.note: GAO measured real attendance against building capacity over three weeks in 2023. You pay the lease, the heat and the light on the empty desks.

source.label: GAO-23-107060, Federal Real Property

items.label: the spending rate in the last week of the year, before the budget expires
items.note: An agency loses whatever it has not spent by 30 September, so it spends it. Two economists tracked the quality of $130 billion of federal IT projects. The ones bought in that last week were 2.2 to 5.6 times more likely to score below the middle of the pack.

source.label: Liebman and Mahoney, American Economic Review, 2017

items.label: still on the table from duplicate and overlapping programmes
items.note: GAO has published a list of them every year since 2011. Acting on the earlier lists has already saved $725 billion. This much is left, named and costed, waiting for a Congress that wants it.

source.label: GAO, 2025 duplication and cost savings report

items.label: of the money stolen from the government every year
items.note: GAO made the first government-wide estimate of fraud in 2024, on 2018 to 2022 data. The answer was $233 billion to $521 billion a year: three to seven cents of every federal dollar. This card uses the low end.

source.label: GAO-24-105833, Fraud Risk Management

items.label: your household's share of the pandemic business loans that went to fraudsters
items.note: The Small Business Administration's own inspector general puts more than $200 billion of COVID business loans in the hands of potentially fraudulent actors. That is at least 17 cents of every dollar those programmes paid out. About $30 billion has been seized or returned.

source.label: SBA OIG 23-09, COVID-19 Pandemic EIDL and PPP Loan Fraud Landscape

items.label: your household's share of the unemployment money that was simply stolen
items.note: GAO puts pandemic unemployment fraud between $100 billion and $135 billion. This card uses the low end. States have clawed back about $1.2 billion of it.

source.label: GAO-23-106696, Unemployment Insurance

items.label: audits the Pentagon has failed, out of every one it has ever taken
items.note: Congress ordered an annual audit from 2018. The Department of Defense has never passed one, and it is the only one of the 24 major agencies that never has. The 2025 audit covered $4.65 trillion of assets and found 26 material weaknesses. The department now says it will pass by 2028.

source.label: CRS IF12627, Defense Primer: FY2025 Department of Defense Audit Results

items.label: your household's share of what was wasted rebuilding Afghanistan
items.note: The Afghanistan watchdog shut for good on 31 January 2026. Its final report counted 1,327 instances of waste, fraud and abuse, and at least $26 billion lost, out of $148.21 billion appropriated.

source.label: SIGAR, Final Report, December 2025 (archived)

items.label: your household's share of the equipment handed to the Taliban
items.note: About $7.1 billion of equipment bought for the Afghan forces was left behind in August 2021: rifles, night vision, armoured vehicles, aircraft. The same watchdog says it now forms the core of the Taliban's security apparatus.

source.label: SIGAR, Final Report, December 2025 (archived)

items.label: the markup Boeing charged the Air Force on one soap dispenser
items.note: The Pentagon's inspector general checked the price of 46 spare parts for the C-17 transport aircraft. Twelve were overpriced. The lavatory soap dispenser alone cost the Air Force $149,072 more than a fair price.

source.label: DODIG-2025-009, audit of C-17 spare parts pricing

items.label: for one filling station in Afghanistan that should have cost $500,000
items.note: A Pentagon task force built a compressed natural gas station at Sheberghan between 2011 and 2014. The same station in Pakistan costs no more than $500,000. Overheads alone came to $30 million. The Department of Defense told the auditor it could not explain the cost.

source.label: SIGAR-16-2-SP, DoD's Compressed Natural Gas Filling Station in Afghanistan (archived)

items.label: what 16 cargo planes that cost $549 million sold for as scrap
items.note: The Air Force bought 20 Italian G222 transports for the Afghan Air Force in 2008. They were unreliable, and Afghan pilots called them unsafe. Sixteen were sold for scrap in 2014, at about six cents a pound. Nobody was held to account.

source.label: SIGAR 21-21-SP, G222 Aircraft Program in Afghanistan

items.label: for one launch of the Space Launch System rocket, a price NASA's own auditor calls unsustainable
items.note: NASA's inspector general priced each of the first four Artemis launches at $4.1 billion: the rocket, the capsule and the ground operations together. He used the word unsustainable to Congress. Nothing is recovered. Every launch destroys the rocket.

source.label: NASA OIG, testimony to the House Subcommittee on Space and Aeronautics

items.singular: JDAM kit, turning a dumb bomb into a guided one
items.plural: JDAM kits, turning dumb bombs into guided ones
items.note: About {price} a kit at the Air Force's largest buys, rising above $80,000 when they order fewer. Reported against the 2024 Boeing contract. Each one is used once.

source.label: Defense News, Boeing JDAM contract

items.note: About {price} for a basic high-explosive round, the figure US officials give. A gun crew can fire this many in an afternoon.

source.label: FY2026 Procurement of Ammunition, Army, justification book

items.singular: hour of an F-35 in the air
items.plural: hours of an F-35 in the air
items.note: {price} an hour, everything counted: fuel, parts, contractors, overhead. One hour.

source.label: GAO-24-106703, F-35 Sustainment

items.singular: year of holding one person in federal prison
items.plural: years of holding one person in federal prison
items.note: {price} a year. The Bureau of Prisons publishes this figure itself, in the Federal Register.

source.label: Annual Determination of Average Cost of Incarceration Fee, FY2024

items.label: your household's share of the F-35 programme, from drawing board to scrapyard
items.note: GAO now puts the lifetime cost above $2 trillion, up from $1.7 trillion, while the plan is to fly the fleet less than before. About $442 billion buys the aircraft. The other $1.6 trillion keeps them flying to 2088.

source.label: GAO, The F-35 Will Now Exceed $2 Trillion

items.label: civilians killed by US airstrikes every day, on average, for twenty years
items.note: Airwars counted the strikes and the local casualty reports in Afghanistan, Iraq, Syria, Yemen, Somalia, Pakistan and Libya, from 2001 to 2021. It puts civilian deaths from US actions between 22,679 and 48,308. Spread over the 7,305 days of those twenty years, that is three to seven people a day, every day. The US military flew at least 91,340 airstrikes in that time.

source.label: Airwars, twenty-year assessment of US civilian harm

items.label: your household's share of the wars fought since 2001
items.note: About $8 trillion. At least 940,000 people died in the direct violence: civilians, soldiers on every side, contractors, journalists and aid workers.

source.label: Costs of War, Brown University

items.label: if your Social Security tax had stayed yours
items.note: The average retired worker collects {price} a year, and half collect less. Your own benefit depends on an earnings history this page never asks for.

source.label: SSA, average monthly benefit for a retired worker

items.label: the year the trust fund empties and benefits are cut by law
items.note: The 2025 Trustees Report projects the combined funds depleted in 2034. Income then covers 81% of scheduled benefits. The remaining 19% is cut automatically, with no vote and no appeal.

source.label: Social Security Trustees Report summary

items.label: the legal right you hold over the money you have paid in
items.note: In Flemming v. Nestor, 363 U.S. 603 (1960), the Supreme Court held that paying in creates no contractual right to receive. Congress kept the power to change the schedule whenever it likes.

source.label: Flemming v. Nestor, 363 U.S. 603 (1960)
